definition: Resampling to put an interval on an estimate, and in this archive the practice that separates the sources whose numbers can be read from those whose cannot -- most archived papers report no variance at all. The corpus's instances show what the interval buys. Problem-level resampling at 1000 iterations with a fixed seed underwrites a pre-registered backfire rate of 56.6 percent with interval [49.5, 63.6]. Hierarchical resampling that jointly resamples seeds and problems gives [+3.92, +5.78] on a 4.85-point gain, which is what licenses calling it real; a paired bootstrap stratified by problem and seed gives [2.592, 8.333] on a 5.617-point gain. And the reverse case is equally instructive: a reproduction finds a published 2.5-point advantage with a bootstrap interval of [0.0, +6.3] that vanishes entirely when the evaluation set is enlarged. One source uses question-cluster bootstrapping on a two-annotator expert study to give [6.6, 19.1] on a 12.5-point relevance gain. The archive's operative rule is that resampling must match the dependence structure -- resampling problems alone when seeds also vary understates the interval, and neither is meaningful for banks produced by adaptive search.

evidence.note: Formalizes test-time scaling as budgeted inference over a model's implicit prefix tree, separates three structurally different regimes that a single scalar budget conflates, specifies what a reproducible inference protocol must declare, and releases 1.9 million traces — with the empirical section showing a selection score that makes accuracy fall from 75.56% to 65.83% as the candidate bank grows.
evidence.title: Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning LLMs: Inference Regimes, Evaluation, and Reproducibility

evidence.note: Audits four neuroscience-inspired claims about language models across 17 checkpoints from five families and 0.6B to 72B, and shows that an apparent emergence of concept steerability with scale is produced entirely by uncalibrated measurement -- raw intervention units, the readout metric, and a fixed operating point -- with correcting any one of the three removing the trend.
evidence.title: When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs

evidence.note: Independently reproduces two published reliability methods and stress-tests them across models and domains their authors never tried, finding one reproduces exactly but loses significance everywhere new, and the other rests on a decodable logic direction that a same-norm random direction matches exactly under steering.
evidence.title: Reproducing and Stress-Testing Two Approaches to LLM Reasoning Reliability: Test-Time Probability Aggregation and Logic-Representation Editing

evidence.note: Builds a Parkinson's screen from control data alone using a contrastive activation direction derived from synthetically degraded healthy speech and a nearest-neighbour anomaly score in face-encoder space, and gives a measurable precondition -- positive cosine between the synthetic and real disease directions -- that predicts in advance which modality the steering primitive will work on.
evidence.title: Label-Free Parkinson's Disease Screening from Face and Voice through Mechanistic Interpretability

evidence.note: Measures, under a pre-registered confirmatory design, how often majority-vote self-consistency lowers per-problem accuracy on a hard science benchmark, and shows that two cheap verifier-free gates recover essentially none of the headroom a per-problem oracle marks out.
evidence.title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs

name: bootstrap confidence intervals
